idiom_name: RAII transaction object with shared_mutex commit
implementation_notes: C++ has no standard-library STM but it has everything the snapshot half needs: cheap moves, `std::shared_ptr<const T>` handles that make 'changed' a pointer comparison, and RAII to scope a transaction object. The realisation that fits the language is a `transaction` class constructed at the top of the block, which records read-set entries as `shared_ptr<const T>` plus its observed value in a vector, buffers writes, and in its destructor (or an explicit `commit()`) validates and publishes - with RAII guaranteeing the abort-on-unwind behaviour that C must do by hand. Use `std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>>` (C++20) or a `std::mutex` held only for the swap to make commit a single step. What C++ does not give you is the key property of the original formulation: memory transactions. Intel TSX / IBM's hardware transactional memory are CPU features with a start/commit instruction pair, and they are not portable, are disabled on many parts, and abort silently on any out-of-transaction call - including most I/O - so treating them as a drop-in for software STM is a portability and debugging trap. C++20's atomic wait/notify and the compare_exchange loop remain the honest portable forms.
pitfalls: Copying the transaction object would duplicate the read set and silently break undo ordering; make it non-copyable.
Committing one location at a time breaks atomicity - another thread observes a half-applied transaction between two stores.
Using a plain `shared_ptr<Cell>` (mutable target) forces a deep copy for the snapshot; use `shared_ptr<const Cell>` and replace the whole node so the undo is just keeping the old pointer.
Reading `*c` without registering it in the read set, which is the single easiest way to lose conflict detection and is not caught by the compiler.

Hardware transactional memory (Intel TSX) aborts on any call that might touch non-transactional memory, including most I/O and libc; the resulting abort storms are far harder to diagnose than lock contention.
